content: 1. Sulfonamides should not be used to treat infections caused by group A beta-hemolytic streptococci. In established infections, these drugs will not eradicate the streptococcus bacteria and, as a result, will not prevent complications such as rheumatic fever or glomerulonephritis. 2. Fatalities have been reported in association with sulfonamide administration due to hypersensitivity reactions, agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, and other blood dyscrasias. Early signs of serious blood disorders may include symptoms such as sore throat, fever, pallor, purpura, or jaundice. 3. Renal complications are significantly less frequent in patients receiving the more soluble forms of sulfonamides. 4. Sulfonamides should be administered with caution in patients with impaired renal or hepatic function, as well as in those with severe allergies or bronchial asthma. 5. Hemolysis may occur in individuals with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, and this reaction is dose-dependent. 6. Adequate fluid intake must be maintained to prevent crystalluria and the formation of kidney stones. 7. Patients should be instructed to drink an eight-ounce glass of water with each dose of medication and at regular intervals throughout the day. 8. Patients should be advised to promptly report the onset of symptoms such as sore throat, fever, pallor, purpura, or jaundice while taking this drug, as these may indicate early signs of serious blood disorders. 9. Frequent laboratory monitoring, including complete blood counts and urinalyses with careful microscopic examinations, should be performed in patients receiving sulfonamides. 10. Sulfonamides may enhance the effects of oral anticoagulants and methotrexate, likely due to displacement of these drugs from plasma albumin binding sites. 11. The action of sulfonylurea hypoglycemic agents, thiazide diuretics, and uricosuric agents may also be potentiated, possibly due to drug displacement from albumin or pharmacodynamic interactions. 12. Conversely, agents such as indomethacin, probenecid, and salicylates may displace sulfonamides from plasma albumin, increasing the concentration of free drug in plasma. 13. Sulfonamides share certain chemical similarities with goitrogens. Rats appear to be particularly susceptible to the goitrogenic effects of sulfonamides, and long-term administration has been associated with the development of thyroid malignancies in this species. 14. The safety of sulfonamides during pregnancy has not been established. Most sulfonamides have not been thoroughly investigated for teratogenic potential in either animals or humans. However, a significant increase in the incidence of cleft palate and other skeletal abnormalities has been observed in the offspring of pregnant rats and mice given high oral doses of certain sulfonamides (7 to 25 times the human therapeutic dose). 15. Sulfadiazine is contraindicated in nursing mothers because sulfonamides cross the placenta, are excreted in breast milk, and may cause kernicterus in nursing infants. Due to the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants, a decision should be made to either discontinue nursing or discontinue the drug, considering the importance of the drug to the mother. 16. Sulfadiazine is contraindicated in infants less than 2 months of age, except as adjunctive therapy with pyrimethamine in the treatment of congenital toxoplasmosis.
